questions.title: Refractive error corrected by a minus cylinder axis 180
questions.question: A patient corrected with a minus 2 diopter cylinder axis 180 has:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A minus (concave) cylinder corrects myopic, not hypermetropic, astigmatism; a plus cylinder would be used for hypermetropic astigmatism.
explanations.B: Correct. A pure minus (concave) cylinder with no spherical component corrects simple myopic astigmatism: one meridian is emmetropic and the other is myopic, so only the myopic meridian needs a concave cylinder. Because there is no sphere, it is 'simple' rather than 'compound'. Compound myopic astigmatism would need a sphere plus a cylinder.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Compound myopic astigmatism has both meridia myopic and needs a spherical lens combined with the cylinder, not a cylinder alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Simple myopia is corrected by a spherical concave lens, not a cylinder; a cylinder implies astigmatism.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a pure minus cylinder corrects simple myopic astigmatism.

questions.title: False statement about keratoconus
questions.question: In keratoconus, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a true statement). Munson sign, a V-shaped bulging of the lower lid on downgaze, is a classic sign of advanced keratoconus.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a true statement). Corneal opacity from stromal scarring or healed hydrops can be seen in keratoconus.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a true statement). Corneal topography demonstrating inferior steepening is the most sensitive diagnostic tool, especially in early disease.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement: a Kayser-Fleischer ring is a corneal copper deposit of Wilson disease, not a feature of keratoconus. The keratoconus-specific corneal iron line is the Fleischer ring, which is different. So a Kayser-Fleischer ring does not belong to keratoconus.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the Fleischer ring of keratoconus from the Kayser-Fleischer ring of Wilson disease.

questions.title: Refractive change in early nuclear cataract
questions.question: Early senile nuclear cataract is accompanied by:

explanations.A: Correct. Early nuclear sclerosis increases the refractive index of the lens nucleus, which increases its refractive power and produces a myopic shift. This 'index myopia' can transiently improve near vision, the so-called second sight. It is a classic early feature of nuclear cataract.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A hyperopic shift is not typical of nuclear cataract; the change is toward myopia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Night blindness points to retinal disease such as retinitis pigmentosa, not to early nuclear cataract.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Uncomplicated cataract is painless; ocular pain suggests glaucoma or inflammation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the myopic (index) shift of early nuclear cataract.

questions.title: Refractive error characteristic of keratoconus
questions.question: Which refractive error is characteristic of keratoconus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Regular astigmatism has perpendicular principal meridia and is correctable by cylinders; keratoconus distorts the cornea irregularly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Keratoconus steepens the cornea and causes myopia, not hypermetropia.
explanations.C: Correct. The conical, asymmetric thinning of keratoconus produces irregular astigmatism whose meridia are neither perpendicular nor uniform. This cannot be fully corrected by spectacle cylinders and typically needs rigid or scleral contact lenses. Irregular astigmatism is therefore the hallmark refractive error of keratoconus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Emmetropia means no refractive error, which is the opposite of the progressive ametropia of keratoconus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify irregular astigmatism as the characteristic refractive error of keratoconus.

questions.title: Meaning of hypermetropia
questions.question: Hypermetropia means that the refractive system of the eye is:

options.D: The eye has long axial length.

explanations.A: Correct. In hypermetropia parallel rays are focused behind the retina because the eye's refractive power is too weak for its axial length. This usually reflects a short axial length or an insufficiently powerful cornea/lens. A convex (plus) lens is needed to add the missing power.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An overly strong refractive system focuses light in front of the retina, which is myopia, not hypermetropia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A very steep cornea increases power and causes myopia, the opposite of hypermetropia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A long axial length causes myopia; hypermetropia is associated with a short axial length.

questions.learning_objective: Define hypermetropia as a refractive system too weak for the eye's axial length.

questions.title: Effect of presbyopia
questions.question: Presbyopia causes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Distance vision is unaffected by presbyopia; the difficulty is with near tasks.
explanations.B: Correct. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of lens elasticity and accommodative amplitude, so the eye can no longer focus on near objects. Patients typically complain of difficulty reading and hold text further away. It is corrected with convex reading additions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Uniocular diplopia suggests a lens or corneal irregularity, not presbyopia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lens subluxation is a zonular problem unrelated to the accommodative failure of presbyopia.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise near-vision (reading) difficulty as the effect of presbyopia.

questions.title: Simplest treatment of astigmatism
questions.question: The simplest treatment of astigmatism is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cycloplegia relaxes accommodation for refraction but does not correct astigmatism.
explanations.B: Correct. Regular astigmatism is most simply corrected by prescribing cylindrical spectacle lenses that add power in the appropriate meridian. This is non-invasive, cheap and reversible, so it is first-line. Laser or surgical options are reserved for those intolerant of glasses or contact lenses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Laser refractive surgery corrects astigmatism but is not the simplest option and carries surgical risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Keratoplasty is a corneal graft used for severe corneal disease, not a routine treatment for astigmatism.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cylindrical spectacle lenses as the simplest treatment of astigmatism.

questions.title: True statement about keratoconus
questions.question: Keratoconus:

options.C: Is best treated by eye drops.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Keratoconus is diagnosed by corneal topography/tomography, not by ultrasound.
explanations.B: Correct. Keratoconus is a progressive non-inflammatory corneal ectasia in which the cornea thins and bulges into a cone. This distorted corneal curvature produces progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism. Causing astigmatism is therefore a true statement about the disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eye drops do not treat keratoconus; management ranges from rigid contact lenses to cross-linking or keratoplasty.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Keratoconus is characteristically progressive, especially in young patients.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise keratoconus as a progressive ectasia that causes astigmatism.

questions.title: Definition of keratoplasty
questions.question: Keratoplasty means:

options.B: Transplantation of a cornea from eye bank.
options.C: Excimer laser treatment of the cornea.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Intraocular lens implantation is part of cataract surgery, not keratoplasty.
explanations.B: Correct. Keratoplasty (corneal grafting) is the transplantation of donor corneal tissue, usually obtained from an eye bank, to replace diseased or opaque host cornea. It may be full-thickness (penetrating) or partial-thickness (lamellar). The goal is to restore corneal clarity and vision.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Excimer laser corneal ablation is refractive/phototherapeutic surgery, not a corneal transplant.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plastic surgery of the eyelids is blepharoplasty; keratoplasty concerns the cornea.

questions.learning_objective: Define keratoplasty as transplantation of donor corneal tissue.

questions.title: Association of mature intumescent cataract
questions.question: Mature intumescent cataract can be associated with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A mature cataract severely reduces vision, usually to hand movements or light perception, not better than 2/60.
explanations.B: Correct. An intumescent cataract is a swollen, water-imbibing lens that becomes thicker and pushes the iris forward. This shallows the anterior chamber and can crowd the drainage angle, precipitating secondary (phacomorphic) angle-closure glaucoma. Urgent lens extraction relieves the attack.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A dense cataract obscures the fundus, so the red reflex is lost, not good.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no medical cure for cataract; surgery is the only effective treatment.

questions.learning_objective: Link an intumescent cataract to secondary (phacomorphic) angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.title: Current treatment of cataract
questions.question: The current treatment of cataract is:

options.A: Intracapsular cataract surgery with IOL implantation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Intracapsular extraction removes the whole lens with its capsule and is obsolete; without an intact capsule, in-the-bag IOL placement is not possible.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Removing the cataract without implanting an IOL leaves the eye markedly hypermetropic (aphakic) and is not the standard.
explanations.C: Correct. Modern cataract treatment is phacoemulsification, in which ultrasonic energy fragments and aspirates the lens through a small incision. A foldable intraocular lens is then implanted in the preserved capsular bag to restore focus. This combination gives rapid visual recovery and is the current standard of care.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Excimer laser ablates the cornea for refractive errors; it does not treat lens opacity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify phacoemulsification with IOL implantation as the current cataract treatment.

questions.title: Features of a subluxated lens
questions.question: A Subluxated lens whether clear or cataractous:

options.D: It can be associated with other ocular or non-ocular manifestations.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lens subluxation is frequently bilateral, especially when it is part of a systemic disorder.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ectopia lentis is often hereditary, as in Marfan syndrome, homocystinuria and Weill-Marchesani syndrome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Management is not purely conservative; a significantly displaced or cataractous lens often needs surgical removal.
explanations.D: Correct. A subluxated lens results from weak or broken zonules and may be an isolated ocular finding or part of a systemic disease. Marfan syndrome, homocystinuria and trauma are typical causes, each with their own ocular and non-ocular manifestations. Because it can signal systemic disease, ectopia lentis warrants a broader work-up.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that ectopia lentis may have associated ocular and systemic manifestations.

questions.title: Image position in the myopic eye
questions.question: Myopic eye focuses images (With complete relaxation of accommodation):

explanations.A: Incorrect. Light is not focused in front of the lens; the relevant focal point in ametropia is relative to the retina.
explanations.B: Correct. In myopia the eye is too powerful or too long, so with accommodation fully relaxed parallel rays come to a focus in front of the retina. The image reaching the retina is therefore blurred for distance. A concave (minus) lens diverges the rays so the focus falls on the retina.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Focusing behind the retina describes hypermetropia, not myopia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Behind the cornea' does not describe the retinal focus relationship that defines myopia.

questions.learning_objective: State that the myopic eye focuses parallel light in front of the retina.

questions.title: Correction of hypermetropia
questions.question: Hypermetropia can be corrected by:

explanations.A: Correct. Hypermetropia is corrected by a convex (plus, converging) lens that adds the refractive power the eye lacks, moving the focus forward onto the retina. This restores clear distance and, with the right power, near vision. The plus lens compensates for the short axial length or weak refracting media.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A concave (minus) lens diverges light and corrects myopia, worsening hypermetropia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A sphero-cylindrical lens is used for astigmatism combined with a spherical error, not for simple hypermetropia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A +2 D reading add corrects presbyopia for near work; it is not the general correction of hypermetropia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the convex (plus) lens as the correction for hypermetropia.

questions.title: Standard adult cataract extraction technique
questions.question: The current standard technique for cataract extraction in adults is:

options.B: Extracapsular cataract extraction with hard PMMA intraocular lens (IOL).
options.C: Removal of the lens matter by laser.
options.D: Phacoemulsification with posterior chamber foldable IOL.

explanations.A: Incorrect. LASIK is a corneal refractive procedure and has no role in cataract extraction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Conventional extracapsular extraction with a rigid PMMA lens needs a large incision and sutures; it has largely been replaced by phacoemulsification.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no routine laser that simply dissolves and removes the lens matter; femtosecond lasers only assist selected steps of phaco.
explanations.D: Correct. The current standard is phacoemulsification, which emulsifies and aspirates the lens through a small self-sealing incision. A foldable posterior-chamber IOL is then inserted into the capsular bag through that same small incision. This gives rapid, sutureless visual rehabilitation and is the technique of choice in adults.

questions.learning_objective: Identify phacoemulsification with a foldable posterior-chamber IOL as the standard adult cataract technique.

questions.title: Treatment of a superficial corneal opacity
questions.question: A superficial corneal opacity is best treated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. LASIK reshapes the cornea for refractive error and is not the treatment for an established corneal opacity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Iridectomy removes a piece of iris for angle-closure glaucoma; it does not address a corneal opacity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phacoemulsification is lens surgery for cataract and has nothing to do with corneal opacity.
explanations.D: Correct. A superficial (anterior stromal) corneal opacity is best treated by lamellar keratoplasty, which replaces only the diseased anterior layers while preserving the healthy host endothelium. Sparing the endothelium reduces the risk of rejection compared with a full-thickness graft. A deep, full-thickness opacity, by contrast, needs penetrating keratoplasty.

questions.learning_objective: Match a superficial corneal opacity to lamellar keratoplasty.

questions.title: Typical presentation of cataract
questions.question: Cataract typically presents as:

options.C: Slow progressive gradual diminution of vision.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rapid loss of vision suggests a vascular or retinal event, not the gradual course of cataract.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Field defects point to glaucoma or neurological disease; cataract blurs vision globally rather than as a discrete field loss.
explanations.C: Correct. Cataract develops as the lens slowly opacifies, so patients report a painless, gradually progressive blurring of vision over months to years. Glare and difficulty with night driving are common accompaniments. The slow, painless course is characteristic and distinguishes it from acute causes of visual loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Limitation of ocular motility reflects an extraocular muscle or nerve problem, unrelated to lens opacity.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise cataract as a slowly progressive painless loss of vision.

questions.title: Type that is not a keratoplasty
questions.question: Different Types of keratoplasties include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a keratoplasty). Penetrating keratoplasty replaces the full thickness of the cornea with donor tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a keratoplasty). Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty replaces the anterior stroma while sparing host endothelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a keratoplasty). Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty selectively transplants donor endothelium with Descemet membrane.
explanations.D: Correct. Intrastromal corneal ring segments are inert plastic implants placed within the stroma to flatten and reshape a keratoconic cornea. They add no donor tissue, so they are a refractive/tectonic procedure, not a corneal transplant. Therefore intrastromal rings are the exception that is not a keratoplasty.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise intrastromal ring segments as not a form of keratoplasty.

questions.title: Term for crystalline lens opacity
questions.question: Opacity of the crystalline lens is known as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leucoma is a dense white opacity of the cornea, not the lens.
explanations.B: Correct. Any opacity of the crystalline lens is by definition a cataract. It may be congenital or acquired and is graded by location and maturity. The term applies whatever the cause, from age-related sclerosis to trauma or metabolic disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ciliary staphyloma is an outward bulge of thinned sclera over the ciliary region, unrelated to the lens.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Iris bombe is forward bowing of the iris from pupillary block, not a lens opacity.

questions.learning_objective: Define cataract as opacity of the crystalline lens.

questions.title: Treatment of a deep corneal opacity
questions.question: A deep corneal opacity can be treated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. LASIK removes only a thin superficial layer of stroma and cannot clear a deep, full-thickness opacity.
explanations.B: Correct. A deep opacity involving the full corneal thickness is treated by penetrating keratoplasty, which replaces the entire thickness of the diseased cornea with a donor button. This restores a clear optical pathway when lamellar (partial-thickness) grafting would leave opaque tissue behind. Superficial opacities, by contrast, can be managed with lamellar keratoplasty.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Iridectomy is an iris procedure for glaucoma and does not treat corneal opacity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phacoemulsification is lens surgery and has no role in treating a corneal opacity.

questions.learning_objective: Match a deep (full-thickness) corneal opacity to penetrating keratoplasty.

questions.title: Complication not seen in high myopia
questions.question: Complications of high myopia include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a real complication). The stretched, thin peripheral retina of high myopia predisposes to retinal breaks and rhegmatogenous detachment.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a real complication). Progressive posterior staphyloma and vitreous traction can produce a myopic macular hole.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception: corneal ulceration is an infective/surface disease of the cornea and is not a consequence of axial elongation. High (pathological) myopia damages the posterior segment, so its complications are retinal and choroidal, not corneal. A corneal ulcer therefore does not belong on this list.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a real complication). Lacquer cracks in the stretched choroid allow myopic choroidal neovascular membranes to form at the macula.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that corneal ulcer is not a complication of high myopia.

questions.title: Feature of regular astigmatism
questions.question: Regular astigmatism is characterized by:

options.A: The steep and flat axes are perpendicular.
options.B: The transition between the steep and flat meridian is acute.
options.C: Cannot be corrected by cylindrical lenses.

explanations.A: Correct. In regular astigmatism the two principal meridia, the steepest and the flattest, lie at right angles (90 degrees) to each other. Because the meridia are orderly and perpendicular, the error can be neutralised with a cylindrical lens. This regular geometry is what separates it from irregular astigmatism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The change of power between meridia in regular astigmatism is gradual and smooth, not an acute step.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Regular astigmatism is precisely the type that can be corrected by cylindrical lenses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Corneal opacities are associated with irregular astigmatism, not the smooth toricity of regular astigmatism.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise perpendicular principal meridia as the defining feature of regular astigmatism.

questions.title: Which procedure is refractive surgery
questions.question: One of the following surgeries is considered refractive surgery:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trabeculectomy creates a drainage fistula to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Posterior capsulotomy (usually with Nd:YAG laser) clears a cloudy posterior capsule after cataract surgery.
explanations.C: Correct. LASIK reshapes the corneal stroma with an excimer laser under a lamellar flap to change the eye's refractive power. By altering corneal curvature it corrects myopia, hypermetropia and astigmatism, which is the defining aim of refractive surgery. The other listed operations target pressure, capsule or vitreous, not the refractive state.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitrectomy removes vitreous gel to treat retinal and vitreous disease, not refractive error.

questions.learning_objective: Identify LASIK as a refractive (keratorefractive) surgery.

questions.title: Wrong statement about keratoconus
questions.question: Regarding keratoconus, choose the WRONG answer:

options.A: It is conical thinning and protrusion of the cornea.
options.B: It causes progressively increasing myopia and myopic astigmatism.
options.C: It can be diagnosed by corneal topography.

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a true statement). Keratoconus is defined by progressive conical thinning and forward protrusion of the central/paracentral cornea.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a true statement). The steepening cornea produces progressively increasing myopia and irregular myopic astigmatism.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a true statement). Corneal topography showing inferior steepening is the most sensitive diagnostic test.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the wrong statement: keratoconus characteristically begins around puberty and progresses through adolescence and early adulthood, not in old age. Onset in the elderly would be atypical and should prompt another diagnosis. Its youthful onset is a key epidemiological feature.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that keratoconus presents in adolescence/young adulthood, not old age.

questions.title: Cause not producing vitreous haemorrhage
questions.question: Causes of vitreous hemorrhage include the following (EXCEPT):

options.B: Posterior vitreous detachment causing retinal tear.
options.D: Ruptured neovascularization at the disc or elsewhere in retina in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a real cause). Blunt or penetrating trauma can rupture retinal or choroidal vessels and bleed into the vitreous.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a real cause). A posterior vitreous detachment can tear a retinal vessel as it separates, causing vitreous haemorrhage.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception: extracapsular cataract extraction is an anterior-segment lens operation and does not itself cause bleeding into the vitreous cavity. Vitreous haemorrhage arises from retinal or choroidal vascular sources, which routine cataract surgery does not involve. It is therefore not a cause of vitreous haemorrhage.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a real cause). Fragile new vessels of proliferative diabetic retinopathy rupture easily and are a leading cause of vitreous haemorrhage.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that extracapsular cataract extraction is not a cause of vitreous haemorrhage.

questions.title: True statement about cataract
questions.question: Regarding facts about Cataract:

options.A: Mature cataract alone can cause no perception of light.
options.B: Intumescent cataract can cause secondary glaucoma.
options.C: Complicated cataract can be caused by astigmatism.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A mature cataract reduces vision to hand movements or light perception, but the eye still perceives light; loss of light perception implies additional posterior-segment or optic-nerve disease.
explanations.B: Correct. An intumescent cataract is a swollen, water-imbibing lens that thickens and pushes the iris forward, shallowing the anterior chamber. This can crowd the drainage angle and precipitate secondary (phacomorphic) angle-closure glaucoma. Urgent lens extraction relieves the pressure rise, so secondary glaucoma is a genuine association of an intumescent cataract.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A complicated cataract results from other ocular disease such as chronic uveitis or retinal detachment, not from a refractive error like astigmatism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no effective medical (drug) cure for an established cataract; surgery is the only definitive treatment.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that an intumescent cataract can cause secondary (phacomorphic) angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.title: Symptom of early senile nuclear cataract
questions.question: Symptoms of early senile nuclear cataract may include:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Uncomplicated early cataract is painless; pain and headache suggest glaucoma or ocular inflammation.
explanations.B: Correct. Early nuclear sclerosis raises the refractive index of the lens nucleus, adding plus power and producing an index (lenticular) myopia. This myopic shift can transiently let a previously presbyopic patient read again without glasses, the classic "second sight". Improvement of near vision is therefore a recognised early symptom of nuclear cataract.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cataract causes a slow, progressive and persistent blur, not transient dimming; transient visual loss suggests a vascular cause such as amaurosis fugax.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Floaters (floating opacities) arise from the vitreous, not from lens opacification, so they are not a symptom of nuclear cataract.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the near-vision improvement ("second sight") of early nuclear cataract.

questions.title: Cause not producing unilateral total cataract
questions.question: A thirty three year old man presented with total cataract in his left eye. The right eye is normal with 6/6 vision. The following may be the cause of the condition EXCEPT:

options.C: Chronic iridocyclitis in the left eye.

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a real cause). A longstanding retinal detachment disturbs lens metabolism and can produce a complicated cataract in the affected eye.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the exception: hypermetropia is a refractive error and is not a cause of a unilateral total cataract. The other options are recognised causes of a complicated or traumatic cataract in one eye. A young man with a dense one-sided cataract should be worked up for local ocular disease or trauma, not for a refractive error.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a real cause). Chronic iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis) is a classic cause of a complicated cataract in the involved eye.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a real cause). Old blunt or penetrating trauma is a common cause of a unilateral traumatic cataract.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that hypermetropia is not a cause of a unilateral total cataract.

questions.title: Commonest cause of cataract
questions.question: The commonest cause of cataract is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trauma causes cataract but only in a small minority of patients, usually unilaterally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diabetes accelerates and is an important cause of cataract, but it is far less common overall than age-related lens change.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypoparathyroidism can cause a metabolic (hypocalcaemic) cataract, but this is a rare cause.
explanations.D: Correct. Age-related (senile) cataract is by far the commonest form worldwide, caused by cumulative oxidative and metabolic change in the ageing lens. It is the leading cause of reversible blindness globally. The other listed causes are real but individually account for only a small fraction of cases.

questions.learning_objective: Identify old age (senile change) as the commonest cause of cataract.

questions.title: Correct statement about myopia
questions.question: Myopia is a condition which is:

options.C: The image is formed behind the retina.

explanations.A: Correct. In myopia the eye is too powerful or too long, so parallel rays focus in front of the retina. A concave (minus, diverging) lens spreads the rays so that the focus moves back onto the retina. The concave lens is therefore the correct optical correction for myopia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A convex (plus) lens adds power and corrects hypermetropia, worsening myopia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. In myopia the image forms in front of the retina; a focus behind the retina describes hypermetropia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Axial myopia is associated with a long, not a small, eyeball; a small eye tends toward hypermetropia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the concave (minus) lens as the correction for myopia.

questions.title: Deposit in band-shaped keratopathy
questions.question: Band shaped keratopathy is commonly caused by deposition of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Magnesium salts do not deposit in the cornea to form band keratopathy.
explanations.B: Correct. Band-shaped keratopathy is the deposition of calcium salts in the sub-epithelial cornea and Bowman layer, forming a horizontal band across the interpalpebral zone. It complicates chronic ocular disease such as uveitis and systemic hypercalcaemia. Because the deposit is calcium, it can be removed with a chelator such as EDTA.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ferrous (iron) deposition forms lines such as the Fleischer ring or a Hudson-Stahli line, not band keratopathy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Copper deposition in Descemet membrane produces the Kayser-Fleischer ring of Wilson disease, not band keratopathy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise band-shaped keratopathy as corneal calcium deposition.

questions.title: Best correction of unilateral aphakia
questions.question: The best option for management of anisometropia in unilateral aphakia is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aphakic spectacles are thick and magnify the image by about 25 percent, producing intolerable aniseikonia when the other eye is normal.
explanations.B: Correct. An intraocular lens sits at the nodal point of the eye and produces essentially no image-size difference, so it corrects unilateral aphakia without the aniseikonia of glasses. This makes binocular single vision possible when the fellow eye is emmetropic. IOL implantation is therefore the best option for the anisometropia of unilateral aphakia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A contact lens is better tolerated than glasses but still magnifies the image by around 7 to 10 percent and needs handling; it is inferior to an IOL for a single aphakic eye.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Radial keratotomy is an obsolete corneal refractive procedure for low myopia and cannot correct the large hypermetropic error of aphakia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify IOL implantation as the best correction for unilateral aphakic anisometropia.

questions.title: Feature of posterior lens dislocation
questions.question: Posterior dislocation of the lens is characterized by:

options.B: Uveitis may occur as a complication.
options.C: Neovascular glaucoma is a frequent complication.
options.D: The ocular refraction shifts towards myopia.

explanations.A: Correct. Four Purkinje-Sanson images are normally reflected from the anterior and posterior surfaces of the cornea and lens. When the lens dislocates backwards into the vitreous, the two images arising from the lens surfaces (the third and fourth) are lost, leaving only the two corneal reflections. Loss of the two lenticular Purkinje images is therefore a sign of posterior lens dislocation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Uveitis is not a characteristic feature of a lens that has fallen posteriorly into the vitreous.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neovascular glaucoma is a complication of retinal ischaemia (as in diabetes or vein occlusion), not of posterior lens dislocation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A posteriorly dislocated lens leaves the eye aphakic, producing a hypermetropic (not myopic) shift.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise loss of the two lenticular Purkinje-Sanson images as a sign of posterior lens dislocation.

questions.title: Cause not impairing vision in keratoconus
questions.question: Causes of visual impairment in keratoconus include all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a real cause). The steepening cornea of keratoconus produces progressive myopia that blurs vision.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a real cause). Stromal scarring and healed hydrops leave corneal opacities that reduce vision.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception: keratoconus steepens the cornea and therefore causes myopia, not hyperopia. Visual loss in keratoconus comes from myopia, irregular astigmatism and corneal opacity. Hyperopia would require corneal flattening, the opposite of the coning seen in this disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a real cause). Irregular astigmatism from the asymmetric cone is the hallmark cause of blurred, uncorrectable vision in keratoconus.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that hyperopia does not cause visual impairment in keratoconus (the error is myopic).

questions.title: Nature of arcus senilis
questions.question: Arcus senilis is characterized by:

options.A: It is formed of calcium deposits.
options.B: It starts in the temporal and nasal corneal periphery and spreads circumferentially.
options.C: It is formed of lipid deposits.
options.D: It becomes indistinguishable from the limbus by the age of 60.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Arcus senilis is a lipid, not a calcium, deposit; calcium deposition gives band keratopathy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The arc begins at the inferior and superior corneal poles first and only later becomes a complete ring, not at the temporal and nasal periphery.
explanations.C: Correct. Arcus senilis is a greyish-white ring of lipid (cholesterol and phospholipid) deposited in the peripheral corneal stroma. It is separated from the limbus by a clear zone, the lucid interval of Vogt. In a patient under about 40 (arcus juvenilis) it may signal hyperlipidaemia, but as an ageing change it is a benign lipid deposit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A clear lucid interval always separates the arcus from the limbus, so it does not become indistinguishable from the limbus.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise arcus senilis as a peripheral corneal lipid deposit.

questions.title: Result of correcting unilateral aphakia with glasses
questions.question: Correction of unilateral aphakia with glasses will result in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A high-plus aphakic spectacle does not itself create astigmatism; its problem is magnification.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Correcting aphakia with glasses does not cause glaucoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spectacle is prescribed precisely to neutralise the hypermetropia of aphakia, so it does not leave the patient hypermetropic.
explanations.D: Correct. A thick aphakic spectacle magnifies the retinal image of the corrected eye by roughly 25 percent. When the fellow eye is normal, the two eyes then receive images of very different sizes, a condition called aniseikonia. The brain cannot fuse these unequal images, which is why an intraocular lens or contact lens is preferred for unilateral aphakia.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise aniseikonia as the result of correcting unilateral aphakia with spectacles.

questions.title: Diagnosis of astigmatism
questions.question: Astigmatism can be diagnosed with:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Placido's disc (keratoscopy) shows distortion of the reflected concentric rings and does detect astigmatism, but it is only one of the listed methods.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Corneal topography maps corneal curvature and quantifies astigmatism, but again it is only one of the options.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. The astigmatic fan is a subjective chart that identifies the astigmatic axis, but it is only one of the listed tools.
explanations.D: Correct. Astigmatism can be detected by all of these: Placido's disc and corneal topography reveal the irregular corneal curvature objectively, while the astigmatic fan identifies the axis subjectively. Each probes the same error from a different angle. Because every listed method is valid, 'all of the above' is the correct answer.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that astigmatism can be diagnosed by keratoscopy, corneal topography and the astigmatic fan.

questions.title: Recession of the near point with ageing
questions.question: Recession of the near point with ageing, making near vision uncomfortable, is termed:

explanations.A: Correct. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of lens elasticity and accommodative amplitude, so the nearest point that can be focused (the near point) recedes with age. Near tasks such as reading then become blurred and uncomfortable. It is corrected with a convex reading addition.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Asthenopia is the symptom of eye strain and fatigue, not the specific recession of the near point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperopia is a refractive error from a short or weak eye, present from an early age rather than an age-related recession of the near point.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The described change is exactly presbyopia, so option A applies.

questions.learning_objective: Define presbyopia as the age-related recession of the near point.

questions.title: Disadvantages of contact lenses
questions.question: Disadvantages of contact lenses include:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Microbial keratitis is a serious risk of contact-lens wear, but it is only one of the listed disadvantages.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a recognised immune complication of lens wear, but it is only one of the options.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Insertion, removal or a poorly fitting lens can cause corneal abrasions, but this too is only one option.
explanations.D: Correct. Contact lenses carry all of these hazards: microbial keratitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis and mechanical corneal abrasions. They stem respectively from contamination, chronic immune stimulation and mechanical trauma. Because every listed item is a genuine disadvantage, "all of the above" is correct.

questions.learning_objective: List infection, giant papillary conjunctivitis and corneal abrasion as disadvantages of contact lenses.

questions.title: Causes of loss of accommodation
questions.question: Loss of accommodation may be found in:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. A third (oculomotor) nerve palsy paralyses the ciliary muscle and abolishes accommodation, but it is only one of the listed causes.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation, but it is only one option.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Tropicamide is a cycloplegic that temporarily paralyses the ciliary muscle, but it is only one option.
explanations.D: Correct. Accommodation depends on ciliary-muscle contraction and lens elasticity, and all three situations remove it: an oculomotor palsy paralyses the muscle, presbyopia stiffens the lens, and a cycloplegic drug such as tropicamide blocks the muscle pharmacologically. Each interrupts the accommodative mechanism at a different point. Because all are valid, "all of the above" is correct.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise oculomotor palsy, presbyopia and cycloplegic drops as causes of loss of accommodation.

questions.title: Retinal change not seen in myopia
questions.question: Retinal changes in myopes include all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a real change). A temporal (myopic) crescent of bare sclera beside the disc is a classic fundus sign of myopia.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a real change). Thinning of the retinal pigment epithelium reveals the choroidal vessels, giving the tessellated or tigroid fundus of myopia.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a real change). Lacquer cracks are breaks in Bruchs membrane seen in pathological myopia.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the exception: choroidal folds arise when the eye is compressed or shortened, as in hypermetropia, orbital masses or ocular hypotony. High myopia stretches and thins the posterior pole, producing crescents, a tigroid fundus and lacquer cracks, but not choroidal folds. Choroidal folds therefore do not belong on the list of myopic retinal changes.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that choroidal folds are not a retinal change of myopia.

questions.title: Correction of myopia
questions.question: Myopia can be corrected by:

explanations.A: Correct. Myopia focuses parallel light in front of the retina because the eye is too powerful or too long. A concave (minus, diverging) lens reduces the converging power so the image moves back onto the retina. The concave spherical lens is therefore the correction for simple myopia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A convex (plus) lens adds power and corrects hypermetropia, making myopia worse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A pure cylindrical lens corrects astigmatism, not spherical myopia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A spherocylindrical lens is used for compound or mixed astigmatism, not for simple myopia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the concave (minus) lens as the correction for myopia.

questions.title: Diagnosis of keratoconus
questions.question: Keratoconus is diagnosed by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fluorescein test detects epithelial defects and tear-film problems, not the corneal shape of keratoconus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An auto-refractometer measures refractive error and may show high or irregular astigmatism, but it does not map the cone and is not diagnostic on its own.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ultrasonography images the posterior segment; it is not used to diagnose corneal ectasia.
explanations.D: Correct. Keratoconus is diagnosed by analysing corneal shape, and Placido's disc (keratoscopy), the basis of corneal topography, shows the distorted, asymmetric mires of the cone. Topographic inferior steepening is the most sensitive early sign. Of the options listed, Placido's disc is the shape-based test that reveals keratoconus.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fluorescein angiography images the retinal and choroidal circulation and has no role in diagnosing a corneal disease.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Placido's disc / corneal topography as the diagnostic test for keratoconus.

questions.title: Symptom of early senile cataract
questions.question: Symptoms of early senile cataract include:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Uncomplicated early cataract is painless; pain and headache point to glaucoma or inflammation.
explanations.B: Correct. Early lens opacities create areas of differing refractive index within the lens, splitting the image so that one eye sees double or multiple images. This uniocular diplopia (or polyopia) persists when the fellow eye is covered, which distinguishes it from the binocular diplopia of squint. It is a characteristic early symptom of senile cataract.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cataract causes persistent, gradually progressive blur, not transient dimming.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Floating opacities are a vitreous symptom, unrelated to lens opacification.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise uniocular diplopia as an early symptom of senile cataract.

questions.title: Sign that is not keratoconus
questions.question: All the following are signs of keratoconus EXCEPT:

options.D: Oil droplet sign on direct ophthalmoscopy.

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a true sign). Vogt striae are fine vertical stress lines in the deep stroma that disappear on gentle globe pressure, a sign of keratoconus.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it is a true sign). Munson sign is the V-shaped bulging of the lower lid on downgaze produced by the corneal cone.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception: a Kayser-Fleischer ring is a peripheral corneal copper deposit of Wilson disease, not a sign of keratoconus. The keratoconus-related iron line is the Fleischer ring, which encircles the base of the cone and is different. So the Kayser-Fleischer ring does not belong to keratoconus.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a true sign). The oil-droplet (or Charleux) reflex on distant direct ophthalmoscopy reflects the cone and is a sign of keratoconus.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the Kayser-Fleischer ring (Wilson disease) from the true signs of keratoconus.

questions.title: Cause of visual loss in lens subluxation
questions.question: Diminution of vision in lens subluxation is caused by:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. A displaced or tilted lens changes its effective power and can cause lenticular myopia, but it is only one mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Tilting of the subluxated lens induces astigmatism, but this too is only one mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Subluxation can cause complications such as secondary glaucoma, uveitis or cataract that reduce vision, but this is only one route.
explanations.D: Correct. Vision falls in lens subluxation through all of these: the shifted lens induces myopia and astigmatism, and it may trigger complications such as pupillary-block glaucoma, uveitis or cataract. Both the refractive change and the secondary complications blur vision. Because each listed mechanism applies, "all of the above" is correct.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that lens subluxation reduces vision through myopia, astigmatism and complications.

questions.title: Astigmatism with opposite-sign meridia
questions.question: On cycloplegic refraction, when one meridian is hyperopic and the other is myopic, the condition is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. In simple astigmatism one meridian is emmetropic while the other is ametropic, not one hyperopic and the other myopic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In compound astigmatism both meridia carry the same type of error (both myopic or both hyperopic), differing only in degree.
explanations.C: Correct. When one principal meridian focuses in front of the retina (myopic) and the other behind it (hyperopic), the two errors are of opposite sign, which defines mixed astigmatism. One focal line lies before and the other behind the retina, straddling it. This distinguishes it from simple and compound astigmatism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The described situation is exactly mixed astigmatism, so option C applies.

questions.learning_objective: Define mixed astigmatism as one meridian myopic and the other hyperopic.

questions.title: Complication of hypermetropia
questions.question: Complications of hypermetropia include:

explanations.A: Correct. A hypermetropic eye is short with a crowded anterior segment and a shallow anterior chamber. This narrow, crowded angle predisposes to acute angle-closure glaucoma, especially as the lens thickens with age. Angle-closure glaucoma is therefore a recognised complication of hypermetropia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis) is an inflammatory disorder unrelated to the refractive state.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypermetropia drives accommodative convergence and causes esotropia, not exotropia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A choroidal neovascular membrane complicates pathological myopia, not hypermetropia.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Posterior staphyloma is a feature of high axial myopia, the opposite of the short hypermetropic eye.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise angle-closure glaucoma as a complication of the short hypermetropic eye.

questions.title: Indication for cylindrical lenses
questions.question: Cylindrical lenses are prescribed for:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Myopia is a spherical error corrected by a concave spherical lens, not a cylinder.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypermetropia is a spherical error corrected by a convex spherical lens.
explanations.C: Correct. A cylindrical lens has power in only one meridian, so it selectively adds or subtracts power along the astigmatic axis. This neutralises the difference in power between the two principal meridia that defines regular astigmatism. Cylindrical lenses are therefore the correction for astigmatism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Asthenopia is a symptom of eye strain, not a refractive error corrected by a cylinder.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cataract is a lens opacity treated surgically, not with cylindrical lenses.

questions.learning_objective: Identify astigmatism as the refractive error corrected by cylindrical lenses.
